HEADLINE: Seven pitched to News but debt a concern
TEXT:
News Corporation fielded a number of pitches from investment bankers to acquire Seven West Media, but the Rupert Murdoch-controlled media conglomerate decided against pursuing a deal for now due to the free-to-air broadcaster's debt burden.

The publisher of The Wall Street Journal and The Australian remains keen on free-to-air television and the potential advantages it could give News Corp's portfolio of publishing, digital and subscription TV assets, as well as co-chairman Lachlan Murdoch's radio investment Nova.

Lachlan Murdoch was part of a joint bid for Network Ten with Bruce Gordon, but the pair were ultimately beaten by US studio giant CBS.

After missing out on Ten, News Corp had a close look at Seven after it was approached with potential deal structures by investment banks. Sources said the approaches were unsolicited and not from banks representing News, although they were seriously considered.

One of the plans was for a scrip offer under which Seven would have been merged into News Corp and existing shareholders in the free-to-air network would have been given new shares in the Rupert Murdoch-run business.

One of key reasons News Corp decided against pursuing a deal with Seven was its debt level of $710.8 million at the end of December.

News Corp made no formal approach or offer for the broadcaster, but sources said it could reconsider should Seven continue on its path of reducing debt and cutting costs.

News Corp and Seven declined to comment.

In February the network suspended its dividend to pay down its debt so it could take part in any potential industry consolidation.

"When something does come along that makes sense for us, we want to make sure we're in the best position to take advantage of it," Seven chief executive Tim Worner told The Australian Financial Review in February.

Seven has been aggressively searching for cost savings, adding a further $20 million to its annualised savings target by the end of 2018-19, taking the total to $125 million. The exception to this initiative is Seven's newly-acquired Cricket Australia broadcast rights, which will cost about $90 million a year, including production cash cost. But the network expects to capture a greater share of advertising revenue because of the cricket acquisition.

At the Macquarie Bank conference earlier this month, Mr Worner said the broadcaster was on target to reduce its debt to about $650 million by the end of the financial year.

At News Corp's third-quarter results on Friday, chief executive Robert Thomson, when asked broadly about potential transactions, said: "We're constantly reviewing our situation and opportunities that may or may not arise. What we certainly won't be doing is paying silly money for overpriced, overhyped targets ... we'll certainly always have shareholders in mind when contemplating any investment."

Seven Group Holdings chief executive Ryan Stokes fuelled speculation Seven West could be part of industry consolidation bringing television and newspapers together at the Macquarie conference on May 3. Seven Group owns just under 40 per cent of Seven West.

"That scale advantage is real. When you've got an ability to leverage audiences across platforms, there are efficiencies. In any deal the synergies have to be there on the cost side, but also how can you leverage that audience across multiple platforms and how do you use the promotional power of TV across different environments," he said.

"For us it's worked well in the west and that model of a combined newsroom works well. It delivers results. We think there are more opportunities."

Seven West shares are up 25.4 per cent since the day of Mr Stokes' presentation. The day prior, Fairfax Media chief executive Greg Hywood signalled his openness to media consolidation, should the right opportunity arise. Fairfax has previously been linked to Seven. However, sources said the two companies are not in merger talks.

HEADLINE: New collaboration bolsters audience measurement for publishers
TEXT:
A new collaboration between The Readership Works, Nielsen and Ipsos will bolster the audience measurement of Australian publishers by bringing it together with television, radio and digital ratings.

Enhanced Media Metrics Australia is the standard measurement for capturing local publishers' monthly audience numbers. Under a new arrangement, EMMA data will have Nielsen fuse print and digital ratings for cross platform audience data and Ipsos will collect print and demographic data.

The measure will include Nielsen Consumer & Media View, which carries product and lifestyle data, as well as OzTam TV ratings, Commercial Radio Australia ratings and Nielsen Digital Ratings, to provide a fuller insight to advertisers on readers.

"We're all bombarded with lots of different sources of data. Media agencies, some publishers and advertisers are struggling to kind of integrate all of these dinosaurs into something that is a coherent whole," The Readership Works general manager Mal Dale said. "It's an important evolution because its also got a much broader suite of audience insights and currency products available for us to integrate, which is a very exciting opportunity for us. What it is going to do is streamline our offering."

Mr Dale said the new currency for readership will allow for greater targeting for advertisers to be more effective.

"A good example, we can ask them what brand or model, what type of vehicle, whether it's SUV, luxury vehicle, and goes down to the individual mark as well. For News Corp titles, they typically profile well against things like Toyota, Holden, things like that ... Fairfax titles, you get Audi, Mercedes, all those kinds of things."

The Readership Works is a subsidiary of industry body NewsMediaWorks and is owned by Fairfax Media, publisher of The Australian Financial Review, News Corporation Australia and Seven West Media.

Nielsen and Ipsos have signed new five-year agreements with The Newspaper Works to work on the enhanced metrics known as EMMA CMV.

"There is nothing more powerful than bringing to life high quality currency data with a greater understanding of Australian consumers' increasingly unique and diverse attitudes, consumption preferences, ethnicity and purchase intention," Nielsen managing director of media Monique Perry said. "We are delighted to see the Nielsen Consumer and Media View client base expand to include News Media and Magazine Publishers."

HEADLINE: Qantas to take Stan Exclusives in-flight
TEXT:
Stan and Qantas have signed a deal for the subscription video on-demand service to have its original programming on the airline's in-flight entertainment.

The new entertainment channel, available on the systems embedded in the chairs in front of passengers, will be called Stan Exclusives and the Australian streaming service will showcase its original productions, such as No Activity, Wolf Creek, The Other Guy, One Night Stan and Romper Stomper.

The deal builds on the partnership Stan, a joint-venture between Nine Entertainment and Fairfax Media, publisher of The Australian Financial Review, and Qantas started last year when the airline's domestic passengers on Wi-Fi-enabled flights received a free three-month subscription.

The aim will be to entice Qantas passengers to watch a show and continue using the service after they leave the flight. Passengers who are not already Stan customers will be offered three months' free subscriptions. Three quarters of customers who sign up under a three-months' free promotion end up becoming paying subscribers.

"It's about being present everywhere so consumers are always reminded of the great new content we've got coming to the platform," Stan chief executive Mike Sneesby said.

"What will be really unique about this experience is that you'll have that ability to access the content through Stan directly before and after the flight and you'll see it in the in-flight entertainment.

"We're obviously also very selective about the sorts of partnerships we do ... you only partner with businesses you feel have an alignment of brand and values."

Stan Exclusives will be available on Qantas flights from June 1.

Mr Sneesby said Stan and Qantas had been working quite closely to make sure passengers watching via in-flight Wi-Fi got the best experience. Qantas' in-flight Wi-Fi leverages the national broadband network's Skymuster satellites. "Our product and technology people have worked closely with Qantas technology people to optimise the Stan streaming experience."

The streaming market is a competitive landscape, but Stan has been able to carve out its niche as the top local player, and second in the market to US giant Netflix. The SVOD service has focused on original productions as well as key strategic content deals, such as with CBS' Showtime, which has given it access to popular dramas such as Billions.

As of February, Stan had amassed 930,000 active subscribers since its launch just over three years ago.

"Financial and brand support of the strategically aligned shareholders Fairfax and Nine Entertainment has leveraged the mass-market consumer marketing reach of both companies," Fairfax chief executive Greg Hywood told investors at the Macquarie conference earlier in May. "Stan is strongly positioned to continue its growth trajectory and, in a changing landscape, is well placed to benefit from the further strategic alignment with global studios and networks."

Stan hit a revenue run-rate of $100 million in November and is pushing towards cashflow break-even at some point this year. Run rate refers to financial data that indicates what money is coming into the business at a particular point in time and then annualised.

Earlier this month, CBS, which owns Network Ten, announced it would launch streaming service All Access in Australia by the end of the year. But it would not launch its Showtime streaming service, given that content was locked up in a long-term agreement with Stan.

In an interview with the Financial Review in April, CBS Studios international president Armando Nunez did not rule out any possibilities moving forward when asked if CBS would consider buying into Stan via cash or content for equity.

HEADLINE: Optus moves to secure Champions League
TEXT:
Optus is firming as the favourite to take out broadcast rights to the Union of European Football Associations Champions League, further bolstering its football offering as a key differentiator in the hyper-competitive telecommunications market.

Chief executive Allen Lew told The Australian Financial Review the rights would allow Optus "to add another string to our bow" as the telecommunications provider tries to become the home of overseas football.

"I think things are happening with Champions League now ... we obviously are interested," Mr Lew said.

"We want to be the home of elite football ... I think you should keep your ears to the ground."

Last month, the Financial Review revealed Optus had again secured the rights to the English Premier League for another three seasons - from 2019 to 2022.

The Singtel-owned telco has been building a home of international football strategy; it is broadcasting every game of the FIFA World Cup in Russia next month, it also has a deal with SBS for the next World Cup in Qatar, and is close to tying up rights to the 2020 European Championship, known as the Euros, also revealed by the Financial Review.

If Optus were to secure the Champions League, it would call into question incumbent rights holder beIN Sports Australia's strategy. The Al Jazeera-owned sports channel, formerly known as Setanta, has struggled in Australia, despite being added to Foxtel's main sports package. It was the under-bidder for the EPL when Optus secured the rights, swooping in and beating Foxtel, back in 2015.

It holds local rights to European domestic football competitions, such as Germany's Bundesliga, Spain's La Liga and Italy's Serie A. However, the EPL is by far the most popular football competition in the world, and losing the Euros, and potentially the Champions League to Optus, could see the Qatari-based company rethink how it approaches the Australian market.

SBS, which already works with Optus on the World Cup and EPL, is also beIN's free-to-air partner for Champions League.

Football has been a key point of differentiation for Optus under Mr Lew, since he took up the job in 2014. While Mr Lew's favourite football team Arsenal, from the EPL, are no longer in the Champions League, having failed to qualify for the second season in a row, Optus' appetite to grab the elite competition has not waned.

The competition brings together the best of the best from competitions around Europe and is seen as the pinnacle of the sport for the athletes, outside of the World Cup, despite garnering far fewer viewers than the EPL.

The second season of Optus' EPL coverage has just come to an end, and combined with a deal it struck with National Geographic in July 2017, it has helped the telco grow its customers base. Over the 12 months to March 31, Optus had its strongest year of postpaid mobile subscriber growth since its 2010-11 financial year, adding 357,000 new customers in the segment.

Telstra, which warned last week its earnings would be at the bottom end of its guidance due to the competitive mobile landscape and poor margins on the National Broadband Network, signed a deal for mobile rights to the A-League, W-League, Socceroos and Matildas matches earlier in May, to go along with its digital rights to the NRL, AFL and netball.

With TPG Telecom's entry into the Australian mobile market expected in the next 12 months, launching with cutthroat pricing, Optus and Telstra are counting on content being a key way to make customers stickier, or less likely to leave to another provider.

Singtel CEO Chua Sock Koong said they did not take competition lightly, following the Singaporean company's results last Thursday.

"We have reviewed our position quite closely. We believe in giving compelling value to our customers, notice I said value not price," she said.

We want to be the home of elite football. Allen Lew, Optus CEO

HEADLINE: Aussies making their mark as diversity grows on US TV
TEXT:
Diversity was a standout feature at the Los Angeles screenings last week as television programmers from around the world descended on Southern California to catch the latest in US network and cable TV shows.

Reboots of cult classics such as CBS's Magnum PI and CW's Charmed have seen more female and people of colour cast in lead roles, a trend that has been slowly building, but stood out in particular this year. "It's certainly the year of diversity," Foxtel executive director of TV Brian Walsh said. "There is an incredible change in the composition of characters."

US networks are "playing it safe" with a range of reboots and spin-offs, Mr Walsh said, including Murphy Brown, Roswell, Suits: Second City and Mayans, a spin-off of Sons of Anarchy.

Ten chief content officer Beverley McGarvey said diversity rang true the entire week, not just in casting, but in writing and production too. "It's really hit its stride this year," she said. "I can't imagine that would have happened overnight - it's very good to see."

Ms McGarvey said she is keen to work with new CBS shows FBI and A Million Little Pieces.

Australians are also making their mark on US television in 2018, with new NBC medical drama New Amsterdam, directed by Aussie Kate Dennis, whose work includes Ten's Offspring and ABC's Rake, one of the standout shows of the week.

FX has also picked up Mr Inbetween, a dark Australian comedy that will air on Foxtel here, for global distribution. The show is directed and co-written by Aussie Nash Edgerton.

Nine programming director Hamish Turner picked out two new shows with Australian actors as leads of standouts. Lincoln Younes, of Home & Away fame, is also a lead in the new Eva Longoria-produced ABC drama Grand Hotel, and Harriet Dyer, of Love Child fame, is starring in new NBC drama In Between Lives.

While US programming is not as popular as it once was in Australia, it still plays an important role for local free-to-air broadcasters, pay TV and streaming services, and they can still pay dividends for local media, on a case-by-case basis.

"It was a long time between drinks for Australia to get a hit. Last year, two popped up with The Good Doctor and Young Sheldon," Mr Turner said.

Seven aired The Good Doctor, while Nine showed Young Sheldon.

"If I'm going to be honest, we're probably in the market for one or two [shows] max, and only if they stand out from the crowd," Mr Turner said.

Gone are the days of long-term and big-money output deals with US studios, which force networks to purchase a list of content, irrespective of its performance locally, and some have been loss-making.

The value of US content has diminished significantly in recent years for a number of reasons, including viewing habits, the impact of subscription video-on-demand services such as Netflix and Stan - which is 50-50 owned by Nine Entertainment and Fairfax Media, publisher of The Australian Financial Review - and piracy.

The trend for local content is not solely in Australia and Mr Turner said US studios were adapting. "A few of the studios openly said they're creating more shows for domestic. In the past, they've had an eye on both international and domestic," he said.

Stan chief content officer Nick Forward said it was clear last year's hit NBC family drama This Is Us, which aired on Ten locally, was having a clear impact on what all the studios were putting out this year.

He also said the ongoing consolidation of the US media sector was front and centre. Disney is trying to buy the majority of 21st Century Fox's assets, with Comcast looking to swoop in, and CBS is in merger talks with Viacom.

HEADLINE: Amazon closes in on securing Laver Cup
TEXT:
Online shopping behemoth Amazon is believed to be close to signing a two-year broadcast deal for the star-studded tennis upstart competition the Laver Cup.

Sources told The Australian Financial Review the Seattle-based e-commerce giant is working out the final details on a deal that would give it global rights to show the Laver Cup, a tournament started in 2017 and owned by Team8, the management company of tennis star Roger Federer, and Tennis Australia, the United States Tennis Association and Brazilian businessman and former player JP Lemann.

The deal would see Amazon broadcast the tournament, named after Australian tennis great Rod Laver, in Australia via its Prime Video service, which launched in 2016, as revealed by the Financial Review, ahead of Amazon's wider launch late last year.

Sources said there are also plans for a range of content outside the matches, including behind-the-scenes content.

The Laver Cup, which is not a part of the official ATP World Tour, pits Team Europe against Team World, captained by Bjorn Borg and John McEnroe, drawing in tennis' biggest stars, which last year included Federer, Rafael Nadal, Alexander Zverev, Marin Cilic, Sam Querrey and Nick Kyrgios.

The unique Laver Cup concept saw long-time rivals Federer and Nadal play a doubles match together for the first time. The entertaining nature of the tournament sees the players have microphones while playing and coaching teammates from the sidelines.

The tournament differs in location each year, jumping from Europe to the US. The first edition was held in Prague last year, and this year's will take place in Chicago in late September.

Amazon has been building a set of tennis broadcast rights over the past 12 months. In August last year, it beat UK pay television provider Sky for exclusive rights to the ATP World Tour in the UK and Ireland.

Last month, Amazon struck a five-year deal for rights to the US Open tournament for UK Prime Video subscribers.

Prime Video has historically been a free add-on the Amazon Prime customers who pay a $US119 ($157.44) subscription for free two-day shipping and some discounts on purchases. However, Amazon has in recent times offered Prime Video as a standalone service.

Prime membership is not yet available in Australia, but Prime Video is a separate service for $US5.99. But, overall Prime Video is a loss making standalone business and is viewed as part of the larger Amazon offering.

The move to secure sport is an interesting point of differentiation for Amazon in the streaming market. In Australia, Netflix and local player Stan, which is 50-50 owned by Nine Entertainment and Fairfax Media, publisher of the Financial Review, have a strong foothold in the subscription video on-demand market.

However, Amazon spent an estimated $US4.5 billion on content last year, and sources said the e-commerce giant had plenty of executives on the ground at the New York upfronts and Los Angeles screenings in the last fortnight, hunting down potential show acquisitions.

HEADLINE: Giving birth to a 10lb high-tech framework
TEXT:
I'm no car salesperson, but it's nice to reach a point where the rigour behind our research is comparable to some well-engineered European wheels. The ones I would feel comfortable selling.

I've talked before about our media attribute testing work, mostly about our findings on viewability and attention and a few other hidden gems. But the technology we developed and the deeper stack and analytics framework has been hidden in the background. After presenting this framework in more than 10 countries in the past six months alone, I think it deserves its own moment in the sun.

This journey began a while ago when a global FMCG (fast moving consumer goods) asked if I could help it understand the impact of different media nuances on consumer behaviour, particularly on a sales outcome.

In previous studies of advertising effects, the use of syndicated single-source data, where advertising exposure and in-market buying behaviour are captured for individual buyers, was common. But such data is expensive and lacks the ability to control for mediating variables in the complex media ecosystem that make each media unique.

So we built a system that delivered its objectives and enabled collection of our own single-source cross-platform data. It was a mash-up of other people's technology to deliver an advertising view with discrete choice modelling as the sales proxy. It was clunky, expensive and unsustainable but the methodological process behind the system was solid and it worked.

More research briefs flooded in with greater degrees of complexity. I decided to acquire a development team with computer vision and machine learning capabilities and start again from scratch. This time we built a true technology stack that was agile, sustainable for scale, incorporated greater measurement accuracy and comparability cross-platform.

We call it MATTech (Media Attribute Testing Technology). It can test the impact of different platform attributes against attention and sales in real-time. It does this by exposing viewers to test ads within the test platform naturally and in real-time. Meanwhile, in the background, attention and platform attributes are collected. After the viewing experience viewers are sent to a virtual store to make a choice (or non-choice) from competing brands in the test category. Confused? All participants are Pure Profile panel members (who double opt-in) and download our custom app onto their device: Electron for TV screen and PC, iOS for mobile and tablet. The code in the app will (depending on the research brief):

a) Expose the right viewer to the right viewing session - Facebook, YouTube or other. b) Activate user-facing camera/webcam when the test ad or content is displayed on screen, to collect footage used by our data analytics framework to mathematically estimate gaze and head trajectory. c) Initiate test ad tagging, thereby tracking its pixels, duration and proportion on screen as the viewer scrolls. d) Intercept natural ad load in real-time and replace it with a client test ad, ensuring ad viewing closely matches the original user experience and allowing us to keep the creative constant across platforms. e) Collect additional variables, including device screen size, device orientation, viewer distance from screen. f) Redirect the panel member to the right virtual store that houses the correct test category. After the app has been used it is made redundant. We do not collect personal information.

All the data automatically passes through our data analytics framework which incorporates a custom machine learning model to estimate eye-gaze on screen against the recorded webcam footage. The model is trained to calculate an attention score based on the extent to which eyes were on screen and on the ad, on screen and not on the ad, or not looking at all. From this, we build client outputs. With individual level attention, sales and a multitude of test variables cross-platform and/or device, this is gold standard for research experimental purposes.

We've tested it across 44 groups, more than 12,000 viewer sessions, 70,000 test ads, three countries, four screens and nine media platforms. It's been a very long gestation. But my vision never paled, our team is amazing, the system is seamless and Formula One ready. So, I am pushing this baby out. Besides, I am guessing they wouldn't hire me at Ferrari.

Dr Karen Nelson-Field is a professor at the University of Adelaide.

HEADLINE: How Nine Entertainment turned TV's summer of sport on its head
TEXT:
Inside the deal The factors that flipped cricket for tennis.

A couple of hours outside of Sydney, in the Southern Highlands, Nine Entertainment executives were struggling for a mobile phone signal at a management offsite when they received documents for Tennis Australia's next broadcast rights deal.

It was Wednesday, March 14, and nestled away at Peppers Manor House in Sutton Forest, Nine executives needed to leave the building, walk 300 metres, and stand under a tree in a paddock, to make phone calls.

Tennis Australia's exclusive negotiating period with incumbent rights holder Seven West Media had expired on Tuesday night, and Nine, which for many years had lusted over the Australian Open, were now given an opening many within the broadcaster didn't think would ever come.

The timing was serendipitous and would lead to the biggest shake-up in summer television in more than four decades, with tennis heading to Nine for $300 million over six years from 2020 and cricket heading to Seven and Foxtel for $1.2 billion.

The tussle for rights to tennis and cricket underscores the hugh importance of sport to television. In an era of disruption and audience fragmentation, sport offers one of the few guarantees that viewers will tune in and advertisers will follow. For Nine, securing digital rights was a key component for any sport it acquired.

"Looking at the tennis deal, and the elements of it, there is the benefit of the sport, which is more demographically aligned to where the network is now and is heading," Nine chief executive Hugh Marks says.

"From the nature of the rights relationship, it's one that gives us the ability to work with the sport, in a very flexible way to adapt our strategy to how we take the rights across any platform, to reflect that we can adapt to changing audience behaviour. We're no longer just a free-to-air broadcaster."

Nine believed tennis would not only fit better with its more female-skewed audience, it was a cheaper deal, in terms of rights' fees but also production costs - Tennis Australia runs production and the event is at one venue - and offered fewer variables compared with cricket, even if it was a smaller amount of total hours of viewing. When the weather is bad, the roof is brought over the Melbourne arena, and the chance of a cricket team failing to last the five days of a Test match is not a factor.

Nine's five-year contract with Cricket Australia had expired at the end of January, but no new deal had been agreed. The network believed it would be forced to make a decision on whether it would push aggressively to retain cricket rights, something it had held for 40 years, before having the chance to look at tennis.

But Cricket Australia hadn't put out its tender for the rights until early March and bids were due on Monday, March 19. It forced Nine to juggle bids for cricket and tennis at the same time.

Nine's boss Marks, director of strategy Alexi Baker, general counsel Rachel Launders and director of sport Tom Malone broke off from the larger management group at the network offsite. They created their own "war room" to pore over the tennis document and start crunching numbers of whether they could make a bid for tennis, which would flip Australia's sport summer on its head, work.

Marks jumped in and out of the room, running the management offsite but pulling in different members of the Nine team when their expertise was needed. But Marks trusted Baker, Launders and Malone and the other members of the sports rights team - Brent Williams and Sam Coleman from sport, Georgia Carter from strategy, Geoff Dyer from programming, James Talbot from legal, Sam Brennan and Luke De La Haye from sales - to figure out what sport would work best for Nine in terms of viewers brought in, including the ability to promote shows, and the revenue advantages.

Marks had signalled to Cricket Australia that he wanted to wrap up a new TV deal by October 2017. Nine had been working with News Corporation about a potential deal with Fox Sports, but nothing came to fruition.

"At the time we were pretty frustrated, but in hindsight, the delay was the reason we were actually able to make a decision on tennis," Malone says. "I don't think we thought we'd have the ability to choose tennis over cricket. We thought we'd be forced to make a decision on cricket before tennis became available in the market."

Cricket Australia was also planning a new schedule so international limited-overs matches wouldn't clash as much with the Big Bash League in October and November. Nine's team built analysis which, to them, showed the network's ability to add extra revenue at that time of year, while running its regular schedule was limited - in fact, limited overs international matches would be loss-making before rights fees.

On Friday, March 16, Nine and Ten agreed on a joint-venture bid for cricket, which would have seen Nine retain Test matches, but all limited-overs cricket, international and BBL, would go to Ten. The pair submitted their $130 million-a-year bid on the Monday. Nine would have loved to have secured tennis and kept Test match cricket. However, Marks was upfront with Ten boss Paul Anderson that Nine would not be overpaying for cricket.

That night, Nine's rights team flew down to Melbourne and the next day pitched to Tennis Australia.

Instead of a sizzle reel with Nine stars such as Karl Stefanovic or Tracy Grimshaw, the network's pitch brought together the management team - Marks, Baker, Launders, Malone, chief sales officer Michael Stephenson, head of content Adrian Swift, digital content director Helen McCabe, Melbourne managing director Matt Scriven and Melbourne sales director Sam Brennan - on why they believed Nine and Tennis Australia would be a great fit.

Nine wanted to make it clear they understood Tennis Australia and the Australian Open was about more than sport - it was an event, a festival, with food, music and children's entertainment - and they were on board to join as a partner to boost that further.

Tennis Australia's media rights team, chief revenue officer Richard Heaselgrave, head of media rights Alfonso Medina, senior manager media rights John Gracia, senior legal counsel Matt Nicholas and CEO Craig Tiley were impressed by Nine's pitch.

The sporting association didn't want just a broadcast partner. Heaselgrave, a former NBA and English Football League executive, and his team have been relying less on the local broadcast contract as a revenue stream. Money was one element of what the organisation wanted, but its investment in production and distribution, where it sold its rights across the world, meant Tennis Australia is not as reliant on local TV deals as other sports. In 2017, Tennis Australia achieved record revenue of $320 million, with about $35 million from the broadcast deal with Seven.

Tennis Australia saw this as an important day. Nine had demonstrated they understood what the sport association wanted, with Baker commenting how aligned the two organisations were. "We went into it with a true sense of partnership to build their event and build our broadcast of tennis - it was quite striking," she says.

But a deal is never assured until there are signatures on the page. Heaselgrave was determined to run a transparent and open process, given the allegations Tennis Australia faced over the previous sale of its broadcast rights in 2013 - which resulted in an investigation by the Australia Securities and Investments Commission over potential conflicts of interest. Heaselgrave, who joined Tennis Australia after the 2013 deal, was adamant there would be no surprises or questions following the new deal.

For decades Nine was cricket, cricket was Nine, while Seven was tennis and tennis was Seven. Both organisations had to have faith that each was genuinely willing to make a switch that would turn summer sport broadcasting on its head, rather than being a stalking horse for incumbents.

On Thursday, March 22, Launders and Network Ten general counsel Stuart Thomas received a one line email from Cricket Australia rejecting their joint bid. It contained no other information.

The next day, Marks travelled to Tasmania for a golf weekend with old friends. Playing at Barnbougle, the weather was terrible, it was raining heavily, but the Nine boss was relaxed.

The former boss of production house Southern Star relied on Baker, Launders and Malone. The trio kept him updated as events unfolded, which included overnight on Saturday the infamous Australian men's cricket team ball-tampering scandal, and Marks felt as the sports rights team worked away, he could be that step back, helping to make decisions on an analytical basis, not emotional, in ways that were best for the business.

Baker, Launders and Malone were back in Melbourne on the afternoon of Monday, March 26. They had been in to talk with Heaselgrave, Medina, Garcia and Nicholas, and had missed their flight back to Sydney.

Looking out on the Yarra River, the three were dining at Japanese restaurant Nobu. There was a sense of excitement, but also trepidation. Nine's board was meeting on Wednesday and there was still uncertainty, tennis or cricket, and no final decision had been made.

By the time of the board meeting Marks decided tennis was the main game for Nine, which would ultimately end its 40-year association with cricket. The board gave the tick of approval to make the offer to Tennis Australia.

"I think the deal Hugh did with the tennis has put Channel Nine shareholders in a much stronger position than continuing the relationship with Cricket Australia purely on a cost point of view," said former Nine boss David Gyngell, who is a company director and Nine's largest individual shareholder. "It showed both business prowess and fiscal responsibility, which is a win for shareholders."

Tennis Australia's board gathered and approved the $60 million-a-year deal. However, there were still details to finalise on Thursday morning.

Stuck in traffic between Melbourne Airport and Melbourne Park on Olympic Boulevard in Melbourne, where Tennis Australia is based, Marks, whose flight had been delayed, went through the final details of the deal with Launders, before giving her the go-ahead to sign the new deal instead of him.

"The one big risk for us in the deal is we don't have the tennis next year," Marks says, noting Seven still holds rights to broadcast the 2019 Australian Open.

If the rights remain with Seven, as the network has signalled, Nine is betting on itself to take on the challenge of a summer without sport, which would take a significant cost out of the business for the year.

"It does give us an opportunity to time some things over summer that we might not have otherwise had the capacity to do," Launders says. "If that's where we end up, it's not a bad thing."

The deal has put Nine shareholders in a much stronger position. David Gyngell, director of Nine and former CEO.
